prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms confined at a magic wavelength made possible frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After reading all eight first-round statements and the chair's summary, I keep the single-part prize for optical lattice clocks, with Katori and Ye, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. What has changed is how I argue it. The chair's first question, whether the lattice clock is a distinct regime or the next refinement of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, is the one that decides it for me. My answer is that the new element is the magic-wavelength condition: it removes the trap-induced shift while many neutral atoms stay tightly confined, so that one gets both accuracy and the statistics of a large ensemble. Neither earlier prize rested on that idea, and the resulting step of several orders of magnitude in accuracy, with independent reproduction in several laboratories over two decades, is a change in kind. The case also carries through the credit: Katori made the proposal and the first demonstrations, and Ye's group delivered the record systematic control and the many-body clock. On the redefinition of the second, I treat it as supporting evidence of maturity and not as a condition. The science does not depend on a decision by the metrology community, and the prize should not hand that decision a veto over a discovery already settled in the laboratory. Seven of eight members now prefer this configuration; I do not count that as evidence, and I have tried to hold the preference only on originality, confirmation and attribution.
statement.case_against: The distinctness judgement is a judgement and not a proof, and several colleagues who share my preference say so. A reader who weighs a new phenomenon in nature above an instrument will find Danielsson's point about IceCube real, and I accept that this prize honours a measurement capability. The credit is also genuinely incomplete: Takamoto and other Sr-lattice colleagues in Katori's group, and groups at PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN, made real contributions that two names cannot carry. I have no verified priority record in front of me, only recollection, and I cannot show that the pair is exactly right. The citation wording must therefore be narrow, naming the lattice-clock concept and its record realisation and not the whole clock race. Finally, the redefinition of the second would make the prize easier to defend, and a committee that decided to wait for it would not be acting unreasonably, though I would not.

responses.point: Kroll holds the science to be settled and independent of the redefinition of the second, but names the Takamoto and Sr-lattice contributions and the PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN groups as a limit on the two-name credit, and discloses his research stay in Hall's laboratory at JILA, Ye's institution.
responses.response: I agree with your view that the redefinition does not govern the scientific case, and I have taken that position from your statement. On the JILA stay, I think disclosure is the right and sufficient step: you document no personal or collaborative tie to Katori or Ye, and a doctoral stay in a neighbouring group is not a relationship to the credited work. It does not bear on how I weigh B004. What I would ask of you is the same as of myself, namely that the Sr-lattice priority question be settled on the record and not on recollection. Where I qualify you is on wording: because we both think credit beyond Katori and Ye is real, the citation should say lattice clock concept and realisation, and I would not add Takamoto without evidence in the supplied record, since that would exceed three names only if we also dropped another.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B010 as a single part for MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, argues that the correlated states are a robust and reproduced discovery regardless of the pairing mechanism, and keeps B004 as his first alternative.
responses.response: You answered my round-1 point on prematurity well: the correlated phases do not depend on a single laboratory, and I accept that an open mechanism has not historically prevented recognition. I also accept that the 2011 continuum model is the specific theoretical core and that dropping Bistritzer would be hard to defend. We still differ on timing and credit. The discovery is reproduced, but the allocation is not yet stable, given Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, Cao as first author, and parallel groups, and you yourself call B004 the safer choice. I would ask what you would need to see on credit to be at ease with a B010 prize, and whether, on the evidence you have, you would accept B004 now and return to B010 in a later year. I keep B010 as my second alternative, not as my configuration.

responses.point: Olsson ranked magic-angle graphene first, set it aside in favour of B004 on maturity and credit rather than physics, and presses the committee on whether the clocks are distinct from the earlier prizes.
responses.response: I respect that you set aside your first choice and say it was for maturity and not for the physics. That is the same position I take: I do not think B010 is a lesser result, and if the mechanism and credit settle, it will be a strong candidate. On your pressure about distinctness, my answer is the magic-wavelength lattice itself: the comb gave the means to count optical cycles and the ion work gave control of single quantum systems, but neither gives many atoms at once with the trap shift removed. I add one correction to my own round-1 reply: I said Bistritzer's omission from a two-name B010 troubled me, and I still hold it, so if the committee later returns to B010 I would not support your two-person version.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from IceCube to B004 but warns that the committee may be choosing the more comfortable attribution over the more consequential discovery, and that B032 could be stronger in a year or two as source associations sharpen.
responses.response: I think your warning is the most serious challenge to my position and I do not wave it away. A clue from nature of the kind IceCube gives is exactly what the prize should favour when it is secure. My difficulty is that the source associations are still at moderate significance and, as you yourself conceded in your statement, you could not verify the roles of Karle and Yoshida; a three-name prize on that footing would be contested. I would not call B004 the more comfortable choice, because it also rests on a real discovery about what can be controlled and measured, but I agree that B032 should stay on the list and I would revisit it when the sources are better established. Your answer on distinctness, ensemble and motional shifts, is the one I have adopted.

responses.point: Lindroth, an atomic physicist, shares the overlap worry, asks whether the redefinition of the second is a condition or only support, and prefers to keep the clock prize single and the cold-atom theory case to be judged separately.
responses.response: I agree that the lattice-clock prize should stay single, and your point that Cirac and Zoller appear in both B023 and B016 is the reason I would not combine it with a cold-atom theory part. You asked whether the redefinition is a condition: for me it is supporting evidence only. As the committee member least expert in atomic metrology, I rely on you for whether the 10^-18 claims and the comparison between laboratories are as robust as I think; if you see a technical weakness that I do not, I would want to hear it before the vote.

uncertainties: Whether Takamoto and other Sr-lattice contributors, or the PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN groups, have priority claims that should change the credited pair or the citation; I cannot verify the priority record from the material supplied.
Whether colleagues will accept that the magic-wavelength lattice clock is a distinct step from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I regard this as a judgement and not a demonstrated fact.
Whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second; I treat it as support, not as a condition, but I cannot say how others will weigh it.
I have less expertise in precision atomic metrology than the atomic physicists on the committee, and my account of the history rests on recollection and the round-1 statements.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict update. My documented co-authors and institutions (Gothenburg, Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg) do not include Katori, Ye or any other credited name on the shortlist, and my work on turbulence, stochastic dynamics and neural networks is not close to optical clocks. I note Kroll's disclosure of his research stay at JILA and, on the record, do not regard it as bearing on B004.
